(2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

Prefer predictions in which a usually helpful edit becomes neutral or harmful in a common context, or a usually harmful edit becomes harmless. Avoid conditions that only a few parents satisfy. v.select_rule: Keep hypotheses whose direction goes against the first intuitive guess but which a reported empirical regularity or a general statistical effect (headroom, floor, saturation, redundancy) supports. Drop those with rare conditions or tiny expected effects. Keep variety across edited fields.
v.strategy: Use the retrieved literature to find measured interaction patterns, not design advice: reports that an option's benefit shrinks, vanishes or reverses depending on what else is present, or that strong configurations respond differently from weak ones. Translate each reported pattern into a conditional hypothesis about this benchmark. Write queries about interactions, diminishing returns and context-dependent effects among components. Include hypotheses in which strong parents gain less from improvements and lose more from degradations. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy.
v.rationale: Grounding counter-intuitive directions in empirically reported interaction patterns should give hypotheses that are true but low-prior, at about 25k tokens.
